topics.title: Robert Moses and the Destruction of the Bronx

hook.text: Robert Moses built 13 expressways through New York City. He demolished 250,000 homes to do it.

buildup.text: The Cross Bronx Expressway alone displaced 60,000 residents, cutting neighborhoods in half with a six-lane trench.

discovery.text: Moses chose routes through minority neighborhoods deliberately. He called it 'slum clearance.'

twist.text: He never held elected office. He controlled 12 public authorities and spent $27 billion without voter approval.

climax.text: Jane Jacobs stopped him from building a highway through Greenwich Village. It was his first public defeat.

punchline.text: One man destroyed more neighborhoods than any war. No one voted for him.

quiz.question: How many homes did Robert Moses demolish for his highway projects?
options: About 50,000
About 250,000
About 500,000

topics.title: The Embarcadero Freeway: Earthquake as Urban Planner

hook.text: San Francisco's Embarcadero Freeway cut the city off from its waterfront for 30 years. Citizens hated it.

buildup.text: Built in 1959, the double-deck highway blocked views, killed businesses, and darkened the streets below.

discovery.text: Voters tried twice to demolish it. Both times, highway supporters and commuters blocked the vote.

twist.text: The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged it beyond repair. The city had no choice but to tear it down.

climax.text: A palm-lined boulevard replaced it. Property values soared. The waterfront became the city's best feature.

punchline.text: What politics couldn't fix, an earthquake did.

quiz.question: What forced San Francisco to remove the Embarcadero Freeway?
options: A citywide referendum finally passed in 1988
The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged it beyond repair
Federal highway funding was redirected to transit projects

topics.title: Detroit's Decline: When the City Lost Its Purpose

hook.text: Detroit went from 1.8 million people in 1950 to 640,000 by 2020. A third of the city is now vacant land.

buildup.text: Auto companies built suburban factories. White residents followed on new highways. The tax base collapsed.

discovery.text: The city demolished 27,000 abandoned homes since 2014. Entire blocks have returned to empty grassland.

twist.text: Detroit filed for bankruptcy in 2013 — the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history at $18 billion.

climax.text: Urban farming, downtown revival, and tech investment are slowly rebuilding, but for a much smaller population.

punchline.text: The Motor City was built by cars. Then cars drove everyone away.

quiz.question: How much of Detroit's population did it lose between 1950 and 2020?
options: About one-third
About half
About two-thirds

topics.title: Boston's Big Dig: The Most Expensive Road Ever

hook.text: Boston buried its central highway underground. It was supposed to cost $2.6 billion. It cost $24.3 billion.

buildup.text: The Big Dig took 15 years, displaced 14,000 residents, and generated enough dirt to fill Gillette Stadium 16 times.

discovery.text: Leaks, falling ceiling panels, and a fatal tunnel collapse plagued the project. One woman died in 2006.

twist.text: Despite the chaos, removing the elevated highway transformed Boston. The Rose Kennedy Greenway now sits above the tunnel.

climax.text: The result was worth it — but the process showed how badly megaprojects can go wrong without oversight.

punchline.text: Budget: $2.6 billion. Final cost: $24.3 billion. Both highway and money: buried.

quiz.question: How much did Boston's Big Dig ultimately cost?
options: $8.5 billion
$14.7 billion
$24.3 billion

topics.title: Highways Through Black Neighborhoods

hook.text: Interstate highways destroyed 475,000 homes in the US. A disproportionate number were in Black communities.

buildup.text: Highway planners in the 1950s-60s routed roads through Black business districts because land was cheap and resistance was weak.

discovery.text: Overtown in Miami, Black Bottom in Detroit, and Rondo in St. Paul were all thriving — then a highway arrived.

twist.text: Federal law required 'relocation assistance' but it was rarely provided. Displaced families received almost nothing.

climax.text: The Biden administration allocated $1 billion in 2021 to reconnect communities divided by highways.

punchline.text: Highways didn't just move through neighborhoods. They erased them.

quiz.question: Why were highways often routed through Black neighborhoods?
options: Those areas had the flattest terrain for road construction
Land was cheaper and political resistance was weaker there
Federal regulations required routes through urban centers

topics.title: The I-81 Debate in Syracuse

hook.text: Syracuse, New York is tearing down I-81 — a highway that split the city and destroyed its Black neighborhood.

buildup.text: Built in 1959, the highway demolished the 15th Ward, scattering a thriving Black community of 2,600 families.

discovery.text: The viaduct is now structurally failing. The city must choose: rebuild the highway or remove it entirely.

twist.text: Suburban commuters want the highway rebuilt. City residents want a boulevard. The debate lasted 20 years.

climax.text: In 2023, demolition began. A boulevard with parks will reconnect the neighborhood the highway divided.

punchline.text: It took 64 years to undo what took two years to build.

quiz.question: What happened to Syracuse's 15th Ward when I-81 was built?
options: It was preserved as a historic district alongside the highway
A thriving Black community of 2,600 families was demolished and scattered
Residents were relocated to new public housing near the highway

topics.title: Cabrini-Green: Chicago's Vertical Ghetto

hook.text: Cabrini-Green had 15,000 residents in 23 high-rise towers on Chicago's Near North Side. It became a symbol of failure.

buildup.text: Built in the 1940s-60s, the project concentrated poverty in towers with broken elevators, no heat, and gang control.

discovery.text: The failure wasn't architecture. It was policy — no maintenance funding, no jobs program, no mixed income.

twist.text: When the towers were demolished, residents were promised replacement housing. Most never received it.

climax.text: Luxury condos and a Target now sit where Cabrini-Green stood. The land was valuable — the people weren't.

punchline.text: Tear down public housing. Build luxury condos. Call it progress.

quiz.question: What happened to Cabrini-Green residents after demolition?
options: They moved into new mixed-income developments on the same site
Most never received the replacement housing they were promised
They were relocated to newly renovated public housing nearby

topics.title: The Kowloon Walled City

hook.text: Kowloon Walled City housed 33,000 people in 6.5 acres — the densest place on Earth. No government controlled it.

buildup.text: A jurisdictional loophole left it ungoverned. Residents built upward — 14 stories high — with no building codes.

discovery.text: Inside: dentists, factories, temples, schools, and drug dens. It was a functioning city without any planning.

twist.text: Residents didn't want to leave. Despite the conditions, a tight-knit community had evolved over 40 years.

climax.text: It was demolished in 1994 and replaced by a park. Nothing else like it has existed before or since.

punchline.text: No planning. No government. 33,000 people made it work anyway.

quiz.question: What made Kowloon Walled City unique?
options: It was the first entirely solar-powered community in Asia
It was an ungoverned, self-built city with extreme density and no codes
It was designed by a famous architect as an experimental community

topics.title: Grenfell Tower: When Safety Codes Fail

hook.text: On June 14, 2017, Grenfell Tower in London caught fire. 72 people died. The cladding was supposed to be safe.

buildup.text: The tower was clad with aluminum composite panels to make it look nicer from the outside. They were flammable.

discovery.text: Residents had warned the management company for years about fire safety. Every complaint was ignored.

twist.text: The government had deregulated building inspections to cut costs. Private firms replaced public inspectors.

climax.text: An inquiry found systemic failures. 400+ buildings in the UK still have similar dangerous cladding today.

punchline.text: They made the building look better. They made it deadly.

quiz.question: What caused the rapid spread of fire at Grenfell Tower?
options: Faulty electrical wiring throughout the building
Flammable aluminum composite cladding on the exterior
A gas leak in the basement that exploded during the fire

topics.title: Le Corbusier's Plan Voisin: The City That Wasn't Built

hook.text: In 1925, Le Corbusier proposed demolishing central Paris and replacing it with 60-story cruciform towers.

buildup.text: Plan Voisin would have erased the Marais district. Streets would become highways. People would live in identical towers.

discovery.text: He saw old neighborhoods as disease-ridden chaos. His solution: light, air, and geometric perfection.

twist.text: Paris rejected it. But Brasília, Chandigarh, and Soviet housing blocks all followed his principles exactly.

climax.text: The towers-in-a-park model failed almost everywhere. People need streets, shops, and messy vitality.

punchline.text: He wanted to demolish Paris. Paris said no. Others said yes — and regretted it.

quiz.question: What did Le Corbusier's Plan Voisin propose for Paris?
options: Building a network of underground highways beneath the city
Demolishing central Paris and replacing it with high-rise towers
Creating a ring of new satellite cities around the existing center

topics.title: Dharavi: Is the 'Slum' Really a Problem?

hook.text: Dharavi in Mumbai houses one million people in 535 acres. Outsiders call it a slum. Inside, it's a $1 billion economy.

buildup.text: 15,000 single-room factories produce pottery, leather goods, and recycled materials. Employment rate: nearly 100%.

discovery.text: Dharavi is walkable, mixed-use, and self-organized — everything modern urbanists say a neighborhood should be.

twist.text: India plans to demolish it and build high-rises. Residents will lose their workshops and micro-economies.

climax.text: Urbanists now argue for upgrading informal settlements in place, not replacing them with towers.

punchline.text: It looks like failure from outside. It works from inside.

quiz.question: What is Dharavi's annual economic output?
options: About $100 million
About $1 billion
About $10 billion

topics.title: The Flint Water Crisis

hook.text: In 2014, Flint, Michigan switched water sources to save money. Lead poisoned 100,000 residents for 18 months.

buildup.text: The new source corroded old lead pipes. Officials knew but told residents the water was safe to drink.

discovery.text: Children's blood lead levels doubled. Lead causes permanent brain damage — there is no safe level for children.

twist.text: Flint is 57% Black and deeply impoverished. Experts say the crisis would never have happened in a wealthy white city.

climax.text: Criminal charges were filed against nine officials. Most had charges dropped. The pipes are still being replaced.

punchline.text: They poisoned a city to save $5 million. The cleanup cost $600 million.

quiz.question: Why did the Flint water crisis happen?
options: A natural disaster contaminated the city's main reservoir
A cost-cutting water source switch corroded old lead pipes
Industrial pollution leaked into the groundwater supply

topics.title: Brasília: A Capital Without a Soul

hook.text: Brasília was built from scratch in 41 months. From the air, it looks like an airplane. From the ground, it feels empty.

buildup.text: Oscar Niemeyer designed stunning buildings. Lúcio Costa planned wide boulevards. They forgot about people.

discovery.text: Superblocks separated residential from commercial zones. Walking anywhere takes forever. Streets have no life.

twist.text: Workers who built Brasília weren't allowed to live in it. They formed satellite cities on the outskirts — unplanned.

climax.text: Brasília is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Residents say it's beautiful to visit and terrible to live in.

punchline.text: Perfect from the sky. Lonely on the ground.

quiz.question: What is the main criticism of Brasília's urban design?
options: The buildings are poorly constructed and deteriorating
Separated zones and wide boulevards make it unwalkable and lifeless
The climate is too harsh for comfortable outdoor activity

topics.title: Ordos Kangbashi: China's Ghost City

hook.text: China built a city for one million people in Inner Mongolia. For years, almost nobody moved there.

buildup.text: Kangbashi had museums, stadiums, and apartment towers. It lacked one thing: reasons for people to come.

discovery.text: China built dozens of ghost cities using real estate as an economic engine. GDP grew; residents didn't come.

twist.text: Kangbashi is slowly filling up — schools, government offices, and subsidies have pulled 100,000 residents in.

climax.text: The lesson: you can build a city, but you can't build a reason to live there. Jobs come first.

punchline.text: Build it and they will come. Eventually. Maybe.

quiz.question: Why did Ordos Kangbashi initially remain empty?
options: Construction defects made the buildings uninhabitable
It had infrastructure but no jobs or reasons for people to move there
Government restrictions prevented citizens from relocating

topics.title: King Abdullah Economic City: Saudi Arabia's Unfinished Dream

hook.text: Saudi Arabia announced a $100 billion city for 2 million people in 2005. By 2024, fewer than 10,000 live there.

buildup.text: KAEC was meant to diversify the economy away from oil. It had an industrial port, golf courses, and luxury homes.

discovery.text: No major companies relocated. Workers commuted from Jeddah. The residential areas stayed mostly empty.

twist.text: Saudi Arabia then announced NEOM and The Line — even bigger projects. Some call it repeating the same mistake.

climax.text: Top-down cities rarely work. People cluster where jobs, culture, and networks already exist.

punchline.text: A city for two million. Population: 10,000. And counting... slowly.

quiz.question: What was KAEC's original goal?
options: Serving as Saudi Arabia's new capital replacing Riyadh
Diversifying the economy away from oil dependence
Creating a military base on the Red Sea coast

topics.title: The Millennium Dome: A Tent Without a Purpose

hook.text: Britain spent £789 million on the Millennium Dome. It attracted half the expected visitors and became a national joke.

buildup.text: Built for the year 2000 celebration, the dome had no clear purpose after the party. It sat empty for years.

discovery.text: The project was rushed for a symbolic deadline. Critics said the content was like 'a theme park without rides.'

twist.text: It was eventually reborn as the O2 Arena — now one of the world's busiest concert venues. The building worked after all.

climax.text: Mega-events often leave white elephants. The O2 is the rare exception that found a second life.

punchline.text: The party lasted one year. The debt lasted twenty. The arena saved it.

quiz.question: What eventually saved the Millennium Dome from being a total failure?
options: The government converted it into a national museum
It was repurposed as the O2 Arena, a major concert venue
Private investors turned it into a luxury shopping center

topics.title: Olympic White Elephants

hook.text: Athens spent $15 billion on the 2004 Olympics. Most venues are now abandoned and covered in graffiti.

buildup.text: Olympic host cities routinely build venues that serve no purpose after the games. Montreal took 30 years to pay off 1976.

discovery.text: Rio's 2016 Olympic Park is crumbling. The athlete village was supposed to become housing — most units sit empty.

twist.text: London 2012 is the rare success — the Olympic Park became housing, schools, and a permanent public space.

climax.text: Cities are now refusing to bid. The IOC struggles to find willing hosts as the costs become undeniable.

punchline.text: Two weeks of glory. Decades of empty stadiums.

quiz.question: Which Olympic host city is considered a rare post-Games planning success?
options: Athens 2004
London 2012
Rio 2016

topics.title: Berlin Brandenburg Airport: The Terminal That Took 14 Years

hook.text: Berlin's new airport was supposed to open in 2011. It finally opened in 2020 — nine years late.

buildup.text: The fire safety system had 170 critical defects. Cables were too short. Escalators ran the wrong direction.

discovery.text: The budget ballooned from 2.8 billion euros to over 7 billion. Three CEOs were fired during construction.

twist.text: The old Tegel Airport, meant to close in 2011, kept running so long that Berliners voted to preserve it.

climax.text: When BER finally opened during a pandemic, passenger traffic was 80 percent below projections.

punchline.text: Germany builds great cars. Airports, not so much.

quiz.question: How many years late did Berlin Brandenburg Airport finally open?
options: It opened two years late in 2013 after minor fire safety fixes
It opened nine years late in 2020 after massive cost overruns and defects
It opened five years late in 2016 after a redesign of the terminal

topics.title: New Orleans and Hurricane Katrina

hook.text: When Katrina hit New Orleans in 2005, levees failed in 50 places. 80% of the city flooded. 1,833 people died.

buildup.text: Engineers had warned for decades that the levees were inadequate. Congress approved upgrades but never funded them.

discovery.text: Wetlands that once buffered the city had been drained for development. Each mile of wetland reduces storm surge by a foot.

twist.text: The Lower Ninth Ward — the poorest, Blackest neighborhood — was worst hit. Recovery money flowed to wealthier areas first.

climax.text: New Orleans rebuilt its levees for $14.5 billion. The wetlands are still disappearing at the rate of a football field per hour.

punchline.text: They knew the levees would fail. They built the city behind them anyway.

quiz.question: Why did New Orleans flood so catastrophically during Katrina?
options: The hurricane was the strongest ever recorded in the Atlantic
Levees failed and protective wetlands had been drained for development
Emergency pumping stations malfunctioned during the storm

topics.title: Jakarta Is Sinking

hook.text: Jakarta sinks 10 inches per year. Parts of the city are already 13 feet below sea level. Ten million people live there.

buildup.text: Unregulated groundwater pumping is the cause. Buildings sit on water-logged soil that compresses as water is extracted.

discovery.text: Rising seas from climate change make it worse. By 2050, a third of Jakarta could be permanently underwater.

twist.text: Indonesia is moving its capital to Nusantara on Borneo — abandoning Jakarta rather than saving it.

climax.text: The new capital will cost $35 billion. Critics ask: who saves the 10 million people left behind?

punchline.text: The capital is sinking. So the government is leaving.

quiz.question: Why is Jakarta sinking?
options: Tectonic plate movement beneath the city
Unregulated groundwater pumping compresses the soil
Rising sea levels from climate change are the sole cause

topics.title: The Aral Sea Disaster

hook.text: The Aral Sea was the fourth-largest lake in the world. Soviet planners drained it. Now it's mostly desert.

buildup.text: In the 1960s, rivers feeding the Aral were diverted to irrigate cotton fields. The lake began shrinking immediately.

discovery.text: By 2014, the eastern basin was completely dry. Fishing towns sit 60 miles from the nearest water.

twist.text: Toxic dust from the exposed seabed causes cancer and respiratory disease in surrounding communities.

climax.text: Kazakhstan built a dam and partially restored the North Aral. Fish are returning. But the south is gone forever.

punchline.text: They drained a sea for cotton. The cotton isn't worth the water.

quiz.question: Why did the Aral Sea shrink?
options: Climate change caused extreme drought in Central Asia
Rivers feeding it were diverted for cotton irrigation
An earthquake redirected underground water channels

topics.title: Love Canal: Poison Beneath the Playground

hook.text: In the 1970s, children in Love Canal, New York played on a field built over 21,000 tons of buried toxic waste.

buildup.text: Hooker Chemical dumped waste there from 1942 to 1953, then sold the land to the school board for $1.

discovery.text: Chemicals seeped into basements. Birth defects and cancer rates soared. Black sludge oozed through lawns.

twist.text: The deed included a warning about buried chemicals. The school board built on it anyway. No one read the fine print.

climax.text: President Carter declared a federal emergency. 800 families were relocated. The EPA Superfund program was born.

punchline.text: They built a school on poison. The law to prevent it came 30 years late.

quiz.question: What federal program was created in response to Love Canal?
options: The Clean Air Act enforcement division
The EPA Superfund program for toxic waste cleanup
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)

topics.title: Phoenix: A City That Shouldn't Exist?

hook.text: Phoenix, Arizona gets 8 inches of rain per year. Five million people live there. They use Colorado River water.

buildup.text: The Central Arizona Project canal carries water 336 miles uphill from the Colorado River. It's an engineering marvel.

discovery.text: Lake Mead — Phoenix's primary reservoir — has dropped to 30% capacity. The water supply is not guaranteed.

twist.text: Golf courses, lawns, and swimming pools consume vast amounts. Meanwhile, farms use 70% of the state's water.

climax.text: Arizona halted new housing developments in 2023 due to insufficient groundwater. Growth may be over.

punchline.text: Five million people in a desert. The river is running out.

quiz.question: Why did Arizona halt new housing developments in 2023?
options: A recession reduced demand for new homes
Insufficient groundwater to sustain further growth
Federal environmental regulations banned desert construction

topics.title: Venice: Loved to Death

hook.text: Venice had 175,000 residents in 1951. Today, fewer than 50,000 remain. Tourism is killing the city.

buildup.text: 30 million tourists visit annually — 600 times the resident population. Cruise ships erode the lagoon's foundations.

discovery.text: Apartments become Airbnbs. Grocers become mask shops. The city functions only for visitors, not residents.

twist.text: Venice finally banned large cruise ships in 2021 and started charging day-trippers an entry fee in 2024.

climax.text: MOSE flood barriers now protect against tidal flooding. But no barrier stops overtourism from hollowing the city.

punchline.text: The water may not sink Venice. The tourists might.

quiz.question: How has tourism affected Venice's resident population?
options: It grew thanks to tourism-related jobs and investment
It declined from 175,000 to fewer than 50,000 as apartments became rentals
It stayed stable because residents benefit from tourist spending

topics.title: Why Public Participation Matters

hook.text: Jane Jacobs had no planning degree. She stopped Robert Moses by organizing her neighbors. Residents know best.

buildup.text: Top-down planning by experts failed repeatedly — Pruitt-Igoe, Brasília, highway demolitions. The experts were wrong.

discovery.text: Participatory planning invites residents to design their own neighborhoods. The results are messier but better.

twist.text: Public meetings are often dominated by wealthy homeowners. The people most affected are least likely to attend.

climax.text: Digital tools, multilingual outreach, and childcare at meetings are making participation more equitable.

punchline.text: Ask the people who live there. They know what they need.

quiz.question: Why do public planning meetings often fail to represent affected communities?
options: Residents don't care about planning decisions in their neighborhood
Wealthy homeowners dominate while those most affected are least likely to attend
Meetings are held in secret without any public notification

topics.title: Environmental Impact Assessments

hook.text: Before 1969, you could build a highway through a wetland without studying the consequences. NEPA changed that.

buildup.text: The National Environmental Policy Act requires environmental impact statements for major federal projects.

discovery.text: EIAs force planners to consider traffic, pollution, habitat loss, and community displacement before breaking ground.

twist.text: NIMBYs now use EIA requirements to delay housing projects for years. A tool against pollution became a tool against housing.

climax.text: California's CEQA law is so strict that a single lawsuit can halt a project for a decade. Reform is underway.

punchline.text: A law to protect the environment. Now weaponized to block housing.

quiz.question: How have environmental review laws been misused in some cases?
options: Developers use them to bypass community input entirely
Opponents use them to delay housing projects for years
Federal agencies ignore them for military construction

topics.title: Building Codes: Lessons Written in Blood

hook.text: Every building code exists because someone died. The Triangle Shirtwaist fire killed 146 workers in 1911.

buildup.text: Locked exit doors, no fire escapes, and flammable materials turned the factory into a death trap.

discovery.text: The outrage led to fire codes, exit requirements, and occupancy limits that every building now follows.

twist.text: Deregulation movements push to weaken codes as 'red tape.' They forget why each rule was written.

climax.text: Grenfell Tower proved it: when codes are relaxed, people die. Every rule has a body count behind it.

punchline.text: Building codes aren't bureaucracy. They're obituaries turned into law.

quiz.question: What disaster led to modern fire codes and exit requirements?
options: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911
The Coconut Grove nightclub fire of 1942

topics.title: Resilience Planning: Designing for the Worst

hook.text: Tokyo built its first earthquake-resistant buildings in 1923 after the Great Kanto Earthquake killed 140,000 people.

buildup.text: Japan's building codes now require base isolation — buildings float on rubber pads that absorb earthquake energy.

discovery.text: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake was magnitude 9.0. Almost no buildings collapsed. The codes worked perfectly.

twist.text: The tsunami killed 20,000 people because seawalls were too low. Engineering can't predict every scenario.

climax.text: Resilience planning now includes retreat — moving people away from danger zones instead of building walls.

punchline.text: Prepare for disaster. Accept you can't prevent every one.

quiz.question: What is 'base isolation' in earthquake-resistant building design?
options: Building foundations deep underground into bedrock
Placing buildings on rubber pads that absorb earthquake energy
Constructing buildings with flexible steel frames that sway

topics.title: The Right to the City

hook.text: Henri Lefebvre wrote in 1968 that cities belong to everyone who lives in them, not just those who own property.

buildup.text: The 'right to the city' means access to housing, transit, parks, and participation in decisions that shape neighborhoods.

discovery.text: Brazil enshrined it in law. The 2001 City Statute gave residents legal tools to fight displacement and speculation.

twist.text: In practice, enforcement is weak. Developers still displace favela residents for luxury projects across Brazil.

climax.text: The idea is spreading: Barcelona, Mexico City, and Montreal have all adopted right-to-the-city frameworks.

punchline.text: You live here. You have a right to shape here.

quiz.question: What does 'the right to the city' mean?
options: Property owners have the final say over urban development plans
All residents deserve access to housing, transit, parks, and planning decisions
Cities have the right to annex surrounding suburban areas

topics.title: Managed Retreat: Moving Away from Danger

hook.text: Some places can't be saved. Managed retreat means accepting that and moving people to safer ground.

buildup.text: Rising seas, worsening floods, and unstable ground make some neighborhoods permanently uninhabitable.

discovery.text: Staten Island bought out 300 flood-damaged homes after Hurricane Sandy and converted the land to wetlands.

twist.text: Retreat is politically toxic. No elected official wants to tell voters their neighborhood is being abandoned.

climax.text: Climate change will force retreat on a massive scale. Planning it now costs far less than disaster recovery later.

punchline.text: Sometimes the bravest plan is knowing when to leave.

quiz.question: What did Staten Island do with flood-damaged properties after Hurricane Sandy?
options: Rebuilt them with stronger materials and higher foundations
Bought out 300 homes and converted the land to protective wetlands
Installed seawalls around each property to prevent future flooding
